case.label: C
case.text: C also gives private access with overlapping CIDR blocks, and the stem never says the service must be closed to unknown accounts. The strongest argument is that an open service name is simpler than allow-listing 30 accounts. It fails on the words MOST secure and restrict each partner: allowing all principals and accepting every request lets any account connect, so A is clearly the more secure of the two.

case.label: C
case.text: C sounds plausible because the transit gateway route table already learned the CIDR blocks by propagation, and a reader may think the same mechanism must be switched on toward the VPCs. It fails because propagation only fills transit gateway route tables from attachments; subnet route tables need explicit routes with the transit gateway as target, which is what A adds. D is already satisfied by the propagated routes given in the stem.

case.label: C
case.text: A reader could argue the endpoint policy is the only access control the stem mentions, so widening it to s3:* fixes the denial. It fails because an endpoint policy never grants permissions by itself; the request still needs an allow from an identity-based policy or a resource-based policy, and the role has none and the bucket has no bucket policy. The stem states both facts, so the missing allow is not hidden.

case.label: A
case.text: Network ACL rules that deny the development CIDR blocks would isolate production, and a network ACL does support deny rules. It fails only on the words LEAST operational overhead: rules must be written and kept in step in 10 production VPCs, while two route table designs on one transit gateway do it in one place. Option D cannot work at all because security groups have no deny rules. Minor wording note: option C says associate each attachment with its group's table, and the shared-services attachment has no group table, but option E settles where it is associated, so the C and E pair is coherent.

case.label: C
case.text: A transit gateway with private NAT gateways is a documented way to connect VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks and keeps traffic private, so C does meet the requirement. It is a defensible technical answer but needs two attachments, two private NAT gateways, routes and a translated address range, which is more overhead than one endpoint service and one interface endpoint in B. The phrase LEAST operational overhead decides it.

case.label: D
case.text: A transit gateway centralizes routing and could be defended as the standard answer for connecting VPCs, with the shared-services VPC already one hub. It fails on MOST cost-effective because it adds attachment hourly charges and data processing, and the stem fixes the scale at three VPCs with no growth, so one more peering connection is enough. Option C fails because peering is not transitive.

case.label: B
case.text: The stem mentions Direct Connect and a transit gateway, which can lead a reader to think that an interface endpoint is needed because only interface endpoints are reachable from on premises. It fails because the uploads come from EC2 instances in the VPC, not from the data center, so a gateway endpoint, which has no hourly or data processing charge, is enough and cheaper than an interface endpoint.

case.label: A
case.text: A proxy fleet behind a Network Load Balancer in the hub VPC would keep the existing peering connections and give central control over outbound traffic, and traffic over peering to a load balancer is possible. It fails on operational efficiency: instances must be patched, scaled and the spokes configured to use the proxy, while a transit gateway with a central NAT gateway is managed. A defender can note that migrating eight peerings to a transit gateway is one-time work, which does not outweigh ongoing proxy operations.

case.label: C
case.text: Interface endpoints also take S3 and DynamoDB traffic off the NAT gateways, and a reader who knows that DynamoDB now offers interface endpoints could call C correct. It fails on MOST cost-effective: interface endpoints have hourly and data processing charges in every Availability Zone, while gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB have no additional charge.

case.label: E
case.text: An interface endpoint for S3 also removes the NAT gateway charge for the backups and is a valid way to keep S3 traffic private, so a reader could pair it with C. It fails on MOST cost-effective because the gateway endpoint in D has no additional charge, while the interface endpoint adds hourly and data processing charges. Option B contradicts the stem, which says the transit gateway must stay for the other VPCs.

case.label: D
case.text: VPC peering has no hourly charge, so on price alone D looks cheaper than a transit gateway, and the three VPCs today are already partly peered. It fails because every VPC must reach every other one at 150 VPCs: a full mesh needs thousands of connections and routes, and each VPC would exceed the peering connections allowed per VPC. The stem does not state the peering quota, so the reader must know it; this is the knowledge the twin pair tests, not a missing constraint.

case.label: B
case.text: An interface endpoint in a dedicated shared-services VPC attached to the transit gateway also lets on-premises servers reach S3 privately, and a central network VPC is a common pattern, so B works technically. It fails on MOST cost-effective because it adds a VPC and a transit gateway attachment when the existing VPC, which is already attached, can hold the interface endpoint. Option A fails because a gateway endpoint cannot be used from on premises. One small gap: the stem does not say the VPC has private subnets, but option C assumes it.
